Copies overlap only if both source buffers are in the same pinned allocation
One H2D copy at a time, but a copy can overlap with a kernel
explain: The best practices guide ties this to asyncEngineCount: a GPU with one copy engine can perform one transfer and execute kernels concurrently, while two copy engines additionally allow a host to device and a device to host transfer at the same time. Streams give permission to overlap; the engine count caps how much overlap the hardware can deliver.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
question: A team wants to replace their bi-encoder with a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval over 20 million passages. What is the core problem?
options: Cross-encoders cannot handle passages longer than a sentence
Every query would need 20 million transformer forward passes, because no document computation can be done ahead of time
Cross-encoders need the documents to be pre-embedded with the same model first
Cross-encoders only work with BM25 candidates
explain: The cross-encoder's document token states depend on the query, so nothing can be precomputed. Scoring a full corpus means one forward pass per document per query, which is why it is used only on a shortlist from a first stage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
question: In the listwise softmax view, which candidate in our group receives the largest gradient pushing its score down?
options: The easy negative at -4.0
The positive at 2.0
The hard negative at 1.5
All negatives receive equal gradient
explain: For softmax cross-entropy the gradient on each negative's logit is its probability: 0.331 for z = 1.5, 0.122 for 0.5 and 0.001 for the easy one. The loss focuses on whichever negatives currently compete with the positive.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
question: A colleague stores API tokens Base64-encoded in the database "so they are not in plain text". What does an attacker who dumps the table need to use the tokens?
options: The encryption key from the application server
A large brute-force search of the token space
Nothing beyond a Base64 decoder, which every language ships
The hash salt
explain: Base64 is an encoding with no key. Decoding is instant and public. The tokens are effectively stored in plain text.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse
question: A service encrypts with AES-GCM but uses a fixed nonce of 12 zero bytes for every message. What is lost?
options: Nothing, because GCM authenticates every message
Only the secrecy of the first message
Confidentiality of messages that share the nonce, and the ability to trust any tag under that key
Only performance
explain: Repeated nonce means repeated keystream (plaintext XORs leak) and, per SP 800-38D Appendix A, likely recovery of the hash subkey, which lets an attacker forge tags. Both secrecy and integrity fail.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
question: Why is a per-user random salt essential even with a slow hash?
options: It makes each hash faster to verify
It replaces the need for a slow hash
Without it, users with the same password share a hash, so one guess tests all of them and precomputed tables work
It encrypts the password
explain: Salts make every user's hash unique, forcing the attacker to attack each account separately and defeating precomputation. Slowness then multiplies the cost of each separate attack.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Elliptic curves and digital signatures: the PS3 and CurveBall
question: Two ECDSA signatures from the same key have the same r value. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing; r often repeats
The messages were identical
The same per-message secret k was used, and the private key can be computed from the two signatures
The curve is broken
explain: r is the x-coordinate of kG, so equal r means equal k (for practical purposes). Then the two s equations solve for k and the private key, as with the PS3.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: In the CuTe GEMM tutorial, a CTA calls local_tile(mA, tiler, coord) and each thread then calls local_partition(gA, tA, threadIdx.x). What does each call keep?
options: local_tile keeps the tile mode and slices the rest; local_partition slices the tile mode and keeps the rest
Both keep the tile mode
local_tile keeps the rest mode; local_partition keeps the tile mode
Both keep the rest mode
explain: local_tile (inner partition) indexes the rest mode with the CTA coordinate and keeps one whole tile. local_partition (outer partition) indexes inside the tile with the thread index and keeps the repeats, so a thread gets one element per repeat of the thread tile.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: A host has all 64 cores rented to VMs and 100 GB of DRAM still free. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 GB is stranded: no core is left to pair with it, so it cannot be rented until a VM leaves
The 100 GB is fine: the next VM to arrive can use it
The 100 GB will be swapped out to free space for other hosts
The 100 GB is lost only if the host is a NUMA machine
explain: VMs need cores and memory together. With zero free cores, no new VM fits on this host, so the free DRAM is paid for but unsellable. That is the definition of stranded memory that motivates pooling.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: With demotion enabled, a server's local DRAM node hits its low watermark. What happens to a cold anonymous page that would previously have gone to swap?
options: It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped, so a later access is a slower load rather than a page-in from disk
It is compressed into zswap on the local node
It is dropped and re-read from the executable file
It is moved to the CXL node but unmapped until a page fault brings it back to DRAM
explain: Demotion uses page migration in the reclaim path: the page moves to the next slower tier and the page tables are updated. The program can still load it directly, just with CXL latency.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
question: Why did the Court mention 'damage' and 'loss' when reading the statute?
options: Both focus on technological harms to data and systems, which fits a law aimed at hacking, not at misuse of information people may legitimately see
They prove Van Buren caused USD 5,000 of loss
They define the purpose test the government wanted
They only apply to civil cases, so they are irrelevant
explain: The opinion reasons from the statute's structure: the civil remedy's definitions of damage and loss address technological harm, which would be 'ill fitted' to remedying misuse of information employees permissibly access.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
question: Why is a sinkhole log sensitive even though it only contains infected machines' IP addresses?
options: IP addresses are encrypted keys
It identifies victims, who can be located and exploited by others before they clean up
It contains the malware's source code
It is not sensitive at all
explain: A list of infected addresses is a list of vulnerable, compromised machines. Shared with network owners and CERTs it speeds clean-up; published openly it is a target list. It is also personal data under laws such as the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation, the EU's data protection law).

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
question: In the hash-chained log, why does editing entry 1 also break entry 2's seal?
options: Because entry 2's seal is computed over entry 2 plus entry 1's seal
Because SHA-256 is slow
Because entry 2 was also edited
Because JSON sorting changed
explain: Each seal includes the previous seal. Change any entry and its seal changes, which changes the input to every later seal. Only rewriting all later seals hides the edit, which is why seals must be stored out of the editor's reach.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: A team doubles the weight of Wikipedia in a fixed 100B-token run. What must also happen?
options: Other domains must lose weight, because the weights sum to 1 and the token budget is fixed
Nothing else changes, because Wikipedia is a small domain
The run must be extended so the other domains keep their token counts
The tokenizer must be retrained for the new mixture
explain: Domain weights are a probability vector over a fixed budget. Raising one weight necessarily lowers others, so every reweighting is a trade, and the interesting question is whether a trade can help everything (lesson 4 shows it can).

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
question: DoReMi assigns 5 percent to a domain with 1B unique tokens, and you plan a 2T-token run. What happens, and what should you do?
options: Nothing: 5 percent is a small weight, so the domain cannot be over-read
The domain is read 10 times, which is fine because repeated data is as good as new
The domain is read 100 times, worth about 16 fresh passes by Muennighoff et al.'s fit; cap it near 4 epochs (weight 0.002) and give the rest to domains with unique data left
Drop the domain, because any repetition hurts the model
explain: 0.05 x 2T = 100B tokens from a 1B-token domain: 100 epochs. The fit gives an effective size of about 16.4 units for 100 read, so most of that compute is wasted. Capping at 4 epochs keeps 4B tokens (weight 0.002). Some repetition is fine, so dropping the domain throws away useful data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: Two pages share 85 percent of their shingles (Jaccard 0.85). Their MinHash signatures are split into 20 bands of 5 hashes; a pair becomes a candidate if all 5 minimums agree in at least one band. How likely is it that they are compared?
options: About 44 percent, the chance one band matches
About 85 percent, the Jaccard similarity itself
About 5 percent
Over 99.99 percent
explain: One band matches with probability 0.85 to the 5th = 0.444. All 20 bands miss with probability (1 - 0.444) to the 20th, about 8 in a million, so the pair is compared with probability 1 - 0.000008, over 99.99 percent. Banding turns a moderate per-band chance into near certainty for very similar pairs.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: You vectorize `sum += pts[i].x` over AoS `Point {float x, y, z;}` with 8-wide AVX. What does the ISPC guide say the compiler must do to load eight x values?
options: A gather (or one scalar load per lane on CPUs without gather), because the x values are 12 bytes apart
One aligned 32-byte vector load
Nothing special: the cache line already holds all eight x values
Convert the array to SoA automatically at compile time
explain: The x values sit at offsets 0, 12, ..., 84, not adjacent, so a single contiguous load cannot fill the register. The guide says such an access "accesses non-sequential memory locations", so a gather is required. They also span 2 cache lines, not 1.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages
question: In the Pegasus case, which finding shows the bucket held more than personal data?
options: It contained over 1.6 million crew files
It was open from February 2022
It was fixed three weeks after notification
Its source code contained plain-text passwords and secret keys, which could unlock other systems
explain: Credentials in a leaked bucket extend the exposure beyond the bucket itself: SafetyDetectives warned the keys could let someone tamper with flight data. Personal data and dates matter, but they do not show the leak reaching other systems.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Encryption at rest, layer by layer: disk, database, field
question: Why bind the row id and column name as associated data when encrypting a field?
options: It makes the ciphertext shorter
It hides the row id
Decryption fails if an encrypted value is moved to another row or column, so swaps are detected
It removes the need for a nonce
explain: Associated data is authenticated but not encrypted. Decrypting with different associated data raises InvalidTag, as the demo shows. It does not hide or shorten anything, and AES-GCM still needs a unique nonce per encryption.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
question: What does exact data match add over a pattern-based SSN detector?
options: It finds SSNs in images
It encrypts the SSN before sending
It confirms the number is one of your own records (via salted hashes) and can check for matching fields from the same row nearby
It removes the need for a pattern
explain: EDM compares hashes of found values against hashes of your table, and then looks for secondary fields from the same record, which cuts false positives sharply. It still needs a pattern-based type to find the primary element first.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
question: A vendor returns a PDF titled 'Certificate of Destruction' listing a batch number but no serial numbers or method. What should the asset owner do?
options: Accept it: the title says destruction
File it and close the ticket
Reject it until it lists each device's serial number, the sanitisation method and technique, and who verified it, then reconcile against the inventory
Ask the vendor to add a company logo
explain: A certificate is only evidence if it can be matched device by device to the inventory and says what was done and by whom (SP 800-88 Rev. 2's list). In Morgan Stanley's case, documents that were not certificates of destruction at all went unreviewed.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Batch-dependent numerics and the token that flips
question: You must guarantee that one request gets the same tokens no matter what else is in the batch. Which property is the one you actually need?
options: Batch invariance: each output element's reduction order is fixed regardless of batch size and of the request's position in the batch.
Run-to-run determinism of every kernel.
A fixed random seed attached to each request.
Greedy decoding instead of sampling.
explain: Run-to-run determinism is already true of a typical forward pass and does not help, because the batch changes between runs. A seed fixes the sampler, not the logits. Greedy removes the RNG but makes the near-tie worse. Only batch invariance pins the arithmetic your request sees.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
question: A replica computes its election deadline as `time.time() + random_timeout()`, using Python's real clock, while everything else goes through the simulator. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the timeout value still comes from the seeded generator
Replay: the deadline now depends on wall-clock time, so the same seed can schedule different events
Only performance: real clock reads are slower than simulated ones
Safety of the protocol in production
explain: Wall-clock time differs between runs and is unrelated to simulated time, so the deadline, and every event that depends on it, changes from run to run. One leak like this destroys reproducibility for the whole simulation. All time must come from the simulated clock.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
question: A company locks down its cloud console with MFA and short sessions, but its deploy pipeline holds a long-lived admin key. Where should an attacker aim?
options: At the console, because it holds the most permissions
At the pipeline: anyone who can make it run their code inherits its admin key without touching the console
At the developer's laptop only, since pipelines cannot be attacked
Nowhere: MFA on the console protects every path into the account
explain: Console MFA protects one door. The pipeline is another identity with the same or more power, and it acts on code it is given. Controlling its input or its runner is as good as owning its key.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
question: CircleCI encrypted customer secrets at rest. Why were they still exposed?
options: The encryption algorithm was broken
The attacker extracted the encryption keys from a running process, which must hold them to use the secrets
Secrets were stored in plain text by mistake
The customers' own laptops were compromised
explain: The report says data was encrypted at rest but keys were extracted from a running process. At-rest encryption protects stolen disks and backups, not a service that is running and compromised.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Terraform state: the file that holds every secret
question: A team marks every secret variable `sensitive = true` and says their state is now safe to share with all engineers. What is wrong?
options: sensitive only redacts CLI and UI output; the values are still in the state file in plain text
Nothing: sensitive values are encrypted in state
sensitive deletes the values after apply
State files never contain variables
explain: The real run shows the password twice in terraform.tfstate. To keep a value out of state you need ephemeral values or write-only arguments, or a secret manager referenced at runtime.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
question: A scheduled `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` on main returns 2. Nobody merged anything since the last apply. What does it most likely mean?
options: Terraform crashed
No changes are needed
Something changed outside Terraform: drift that the owners must review
The state file is encrypted
explain: Exit code 2 means the plan succeeded and has changes. With no new code, those changes come from the live side: drift. Exit code 1 would be an error.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
question: In a reverse step from t to s, a masked position stays masked with probability s/t. What happens when s = 0?
options: Every masked position is revealed in this step
Nothing is revealed, because s/t = 0 means no change
Half of the masked positions are revealed
The visible tokens are remasked
explain: With s = 0 the probability of staying masked is 0/t = 0, so every remaining mask must be filled. The last step of any schedule ends at s = 0 and finishes the sequence.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
question: Which metric does a chat user notice first if prefills are always scheduled ahead of decodes on a busy colocated GPU?
options: Neither, since prefill priority helps everyone
Throughput in tokens per second must drop
TTFT gets worse
TPOT/TBT gets worse: running streams stutter while new prompts are processed
explain: Prioritizing prefill keeps TTFT low but every prefill iteration delays the next token of every running request. Splitwise notes that letting a waiting prompt preempt token generation shortens TTFT but can substantially increase the tail of TBT. Throughput may even rise; latency of the other phase is what suffers.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What storage remembers: the BTK floppy disk (2005)
question: Why could examiners read a document that had been deleted from the BTK floppy?
options: Floppy disks keep a hidden backup copy of every file
Forensic software can reverse any overwrite by reading residual magnetism
Deletion marked the space as free but left the file's bytes in place, and nothing had overwritten them yet
The deleted file was still listed as live in the directory
explain: Deletion freed the entry and the space; the content stayed until reused. There is no hidden backup on a floppy, and overwritten data is not recoverable with standard tools. The directory listed only the message file, so the earlier files were not live.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Eight NTFS timestamps, and how timestomping gets caught
question: SI created = 2023-01-10 14:22:31.0000000, FN created = 2024-06-02 08:15:44.3871190. What is the most defensible statement?
options: SI created was probably rewritten after June 2024; corroborate with the USN journal and process telemetry before concluding
The file was created on 10 January 2023
The file was timestomped by the user who owns it
The FN time is wrong because FN is less reliable than SI
explain: SI earlier than FN plus a zero fraction is a strong lead that SI was rewritten, not proof of who did it or why. FN is the harder set to change, so the 2023 claim is the suspect one.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all
question: Your carver recovers a 9 KB JPEG that opens as a tiny 160 x 120 picture, while the camera wrote 4 MB images. What most likely happened?
options: The camera compressed the image after deletion
TRIM shrank the file
The JPEG header was corrupted
The carver stopped at the FF D9 of an embedded thumbnail (nested content)
explain: JPEGs commonly carry a thumbnail that is itself a complete JPEG. A header and footer carver that stops at the first FF D9 returns the thumbnail. TRIM discards blocks; it does not shrink files.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Mobile forensics: extraction levels, encryption and isolation
question: A seized iPhone was found switched off and has not been unlocked since. Which data is most likely readable without the passcode?
options: Everything in Class C, because it is the default
Everything, because a chip-off bypasses Data Protection
Only data protected by Class D (No Protection) and similar always-available items
All messages, because the phone was off
explain: This is BFU: no class keys except D's are available. Class C keys appear only after the first unlock. Chip-off yields ciphertext, since keys are bound to the device's hardware.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence law and writing the expert report
question: Under the Daubert criteria as CyBOK summarises them, which question about a new carving tool matters most to admissibility?
options: Is it the most popular tool in the lab?
Was it written in a memory-safe language?
Has its method been tested, with a known error rate, ideally published and generally accepted?
Does it run on Windows?
explain: Daubert asks for testability, peer review, a known error rate and general acceptance. Popularity, language and platform are not criteria, though popularity can feed general acceptance.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA: a fixed-degree graph built for GPUs
question: Why does CAGRA use rank-based reordering instead of computing distances between neighbors?
options: Ranks give strictly better graphs
Distance-based reordering needs about N x d_init x (d_init - 1) distance computations or an N x d_init distance table, which is slow or runs out of memory at scale
GPUs cannot compute distances
NN-descent does not produce sorted lists
explain: The paper reports that distance-based reordering was slower and hit out-of-memory on DEEP-100M, while rank-based reordering gave almost the same recall-throughput curve. The rank is a free proxy because NN-descent already sorted each list by distance.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
question: With IPO at $\tau = 0.25$ in the two-answer toy, what probability does the policy converge to on $y_1$?
options: 50%, the reference
About 73%
About 88%
explain: The target gap is $1/(2\tau) = 2$, so $\pi(y_1) = \sigma(2) \approx 0.881$. Smaller $\tau$ means a bigger target gap and a more confident policy, but never fully deterministic.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
question: Which step is the real point of no return, where undoing it needs more than flipping a flag back?
options: Starting dual writes
Switching reads to the new store
Switching writes to the new store while still archiving to the old one
Stopping writes to the old store and deleting its data
explain: As long as some code keeps the old store current (dual writes in phases 1 to 3, archiving in phase 3), you can point traffic back at it. Once old writes stop and its data is deleted, going back would mean a new migration in the other direction.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
question: A gh-ost migration's applier is 6,000 events behind and applies 10,000 events per second. Using the simplified model, roughly how long are writes blocked during cut-over?
options: About 6 ms
About 60 ms
About 600 ms
About 6 seconds
explain: 6,000 events at 10,000 events per second take 0.6 s. That is why tools throttle and wait for lag to be small before cutting over: the write pause grows with the backlog.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: You remove the /has_key(@start, tid)/ filter from the timing script. What do you most likely see?
options: Nothing changes
The verifier rejects the script
A few enormous durations near the system uptime, from calls that started before tracing began and read a start time of 0
Every duration becomes 0
explain: Calls already in flight at attach time only hit the return probe. Their @start[tid] reads as 0, so nsecs - 0 equals the time since boot, which pollutes the top buckets of the histogram.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
question: Why does the quantization scheme require that real 0 maps exactly to an integer code?
options: Because int8 cannot store negative numbers
Because zero padding and ReLU zeros would otherwise all carry the same rounding error, acting as a systematic bias
Because the scale S must be an integer
Because dequantization divides by zero otherwise
explain: Zero padding inserts many zeros at borders and ReLU creates many exact zeros. If 0 were not on the grid, they would all round to the same nonzero value, a biased error repeated across the tensor. Jacob et al. and the ONNX Runtime docs both call this requirement out.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
question: Why is a VPN gateway often a more valuable target than an employee laptop?
options: It usually has a faster processor
Laptops cannot be attacked over the network
VPN traffic is not encrypted
Anyone can reach it before login, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it usually runs no EDR
explain: The three properties together: pre-authentication exposure, a privileged position (passwords, service accounts, routes inside) and little monitoring. A laptop typically has EDR and must first be reached through phishing.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
question: Why did the toy on-box integrity checker report nothing on a backdoored appliance?
options: Its known-good hashes were wrong
SHA-256 is broken
It only checks files in /tmp
The intruder had root and edited the skip list the checker reads from the same device
explain: The manifest was correct. The checker trusted configuration stored on the device it was checking. Volexity found the real attacker adding entries to the ICT's files; CISA later found even the external ICT missed compromises.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
question: Which setup meets BOD 23-02 for a firewall's web admin page?
options: The admin page stays on the internet with a long password
The admin page is moved to port 18443 so scanners miss it
The admin page is public but logs every login
The admin page answers only on an isolated management network reached from admin workstations
explain: BOD 23-02 accepts two options: remove the interface from the internet, or put a separate policy enforcement point in front of it. A strong password, an unusual port or logging leave the interface itself reachable.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: A reasoning model's response has 5 solutions; the first correct answer appears in solution 1 (60 tokens) and the response is 600 tokens. A colleague says 'truncate every response after solution 1 and nothing is lost'. What does Chen et al.'s data say?
options: Correct: later solutions never change the answer, so truncation is free
Mostly right for easy sets, but on hard sets later rounds sometimes fix a wrong first answer, and the authors keep one reflection round for that reason
Wrong: later solutions are where most correct answers first appear
Wrong: the first solution is usually the longest, so truncating saves little
explain: Over 92% of correct responses are already correct at solution 1, which is why the waste is large. But not 100%: keeping only the first correct solution (FCS) lowered MATH500 accuracy, so their best recipe keeps one extra reflection round (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
question: Why does s1 append 'Wait' when suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter, rather than just suppressing it?
options: The tokenizer needs a non-empty token after suppression
'Wait' counts as zero tokens toward the budget
Without a string the model tends to emit the delimiter again immediately
In s1's ablation, 'Wait' gave the best scores; suppression with no string lowered MATH500 and GPQA
explain: Table 4: 2x with no string scored 90.2 on MATH500 and 55.1 on GPQA (vs 93.0 and 57.6 without extrapolation, that is, without forcing extra thinking), while 2x 'Wait' gave 53.3, 93.0 and 59.6. 'Wait' reliably triggers a re-check.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: A NetworkConnect filter is `onmatch="include"` with two rules: Image ends with `powershell.exe`, and DestinationPort is `443`. Which connection is logged?
options: Only connections made by powershell.exe to port 443
Any connection made by powershell.exe
Any connection to port 443
Every connection, because include with two rules logs all
explain: The two rules are on different fields (Image and DestinationPort), and Sysmon combines different fields with AND. Two rules on the same field would have been ORed.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: Your draft AppLocker policy has run in audit mode for two weeks. Which events tell you what the policy would have broken?
explain: 8003 (EXE or DLL) and 8006 (script or MSI) mean 'allowed, but would have been prevented if enforced', and appear only in audit mode. 8004 and 8007 are actual blocks in enforce mode; 8002 and 8005 are allows.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: An attacker uses only built-in tools (net for accounts and shares, wmic, and ntdsutil, the Active Directory database tool) with valid admin credentials. Why is this hard for an EDR?
options: The telemetry is recorded, but each action resembles normal administration, so detection depends on context and baselines rather than a 'malware' verdict
EDR cannot record built-in tools
Built-in tools disable EDR automatically
Windows hides admin activity from all sensors
explain: The sensor still records the processes and command lines. The difficulty is deciding they are malicious: CISA's living-off-the-land guidance notes that many organisations lack the capabilities to tell such activity from normal administration, which is why baselines of admin behaviour matter.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
question: At minute 47 the meter reads 122 W. Which statement is correct using only that one reading?
options: It must be the fridge, because the fridge draws 120 W
It could be the fridge alone, or two 60 W lamps if the house had two, so one reading cannot decide
It must be the lamp plus 62 W of noise
It is the kettle in a low-power state
explain: A single reading only constrains the sum. With three known appliances, 120 W happens to match one combination, but adding a second 60 W lamp would create a second exact match. Context over time (what changed, and when) is what breaks such ties.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
question: A model reaches F1 0.95 on houses it was trained on and 0.60 on a new house. What is the most useful next step suggested by this course's sources?
options: Report 0.95, since the training houses are representative
Shrink the window to one sample to avoid overfitting
Switch to CO, which needs no training data
Add synthetic aggregates built from activations of many houses and evaluate on a held-out house
explain: Kelly and Knottenbelt found that mixing synthetic aggregates with real data regularised the nets and helped on unseen houses, and both they and Zhang and colleagues test on a held-out house. A one-sample window throws away the context that makes neural NILM work, and CO still needs appliance models learned from sub-metered data.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
question: Why is a missing domain scored as weight 0 rather than with the disagree weight -2.74?
options: Missing data carries no evidence either way; scoring it as disagreement would push true duplicates like r1-r3 toward non-match
Because log2 of zero is undefined
Because Fellegi-Sunter only allows agreement levels
explain: A missing value is neither agreement nor disagreement. Treating it as disagreement subtracts 2.74 and would drop r1-r3 from 0.863 to about 0.49, punishing incomplete records rather than conflicting ones.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: A SaaS vendor's own tenant is breached, and the attacker adds a new client secret to the vendor's multitenant application object. Your tenant granted that app's service principal Mail.Read (application). What is your exposure?
options: None: the secret was added in another tenant
Only mailboxes of users who signed in to the app
The attacker can get app-only tokens for your tenant and read every mailbox the permission covers, until you disable the service principal or remove the grant
None, because application permissions need MFA
explain: The app authenticates with credentials on its application object, wherever that lives, and is authorized by your service principal's grants. Your controls are on your side: the grant, and disabling the service principal.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: An email asks a user to enter a 'Teams meeting ID' at microsoft.com/devicelogin. The user does so and signs in with a FIDO2 key. What happened?
options: Nothing: FIDO2 binds the sign-in to the correct origin, so the attacker gets no tokens
Only an ID token was issued, which cannot read mail
The attacker, who started the device code flow, received tokens for the user; FIDO2 protected the login page but not the flow
The sign-in failed because FIDO2 is not supported for device code flow
explain: The user signed in on the real Microsoft origin, so the passkey worked. The device authorization grant then issued tokens to the client that requested the code: the attacker. Blocking the flow is the control.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: An attacker has Domain Admin on premises. The tenant uses PHS and Seamless SSO, and all Global Administrators are synced accounts. Which change removes the most direct path to Global Administrator?
options: Switching from PHS to PTA
Disabling Teams
Making Global Administrators cloud-only accounts with phishing-resistant MFA, so no on-premises object holds cloud admin rights
Enabling the AD recycle bin
explain: With synced admins, control of AD or the sync server can change those accounts (passwords, soft or hard matching). Microsoft's rule is that no on-premises account should hold Microsoft 365 admin rights. Switching to PTA moves the bridge to new Tier 0 agents; it does not remove it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: A server handles 20,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections with one thread per connection. Which cost grows directly with the number of *idle* connections?
options: CPU time spent parsing requests
A sleeping thread, with its own stack and kernel task, for every connection
Network bandwidth used by the replies
The number of bytes each request contains
explain: Parsing and bandwidth scale with *active* traffic. An idle connection does no work, but in thread-per-connection it still owns a whole thread: a stack, a kernel task, and a place in the scheduler. An event loop keeps only a small per-connection record instead.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: A Node service handles 4 slow password hashes (crypto.pbkdf2, about 100 ms each) at the same moment that 4 requests call fs.readFile. With the default pool, what do the file reads experience?
options: They queue behind the hashes on the 4-thread pool, so they finish roughly 100 ms later than they otherwise would
Nothing, file reads use epoll and never touch the pool
They run on the loop thread and block it
Node starts 4 extra threads automatically for file I/O
explain: Both async pbkdf2 and fs calls run on libuv's shared thread pool, which has 4 threads by default. The hashes occupy all 4, so the file reads wait about one hash duration. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE or moving hashing elsewhere fixes it. Disk files cannot use epoll at all.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
question: Two systems' per-query nDCG@10 values correlate at 0.9 across 100 queries. Compared with an unpaired bootstrap, what does a paired bootstrap of the mean difference give?
options: A wider interval, because pairing loses degrees of freedom
The same interval, because the means are identical either way
A much narrower interval, because shared query difficulty cancels in the per-query differences
An interval centered on a different value
explain: The point estimate is the same mean difference either way. With strong correlation, most per-query variation is query difficulty that hits both systems alike. Differencing per query removes it, so the variance of the difference is much smaller than the sum of the two variances.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
question: A JIT engine maps one page as readable, writable and executable and keeps writing new code into it while it runs. Which policy does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: W^X, because any memory-write bug could place attacker code in a page that is also executable
ASLR, because the page has a fixed address
RELRO, because the page is writable
None: JIT pages are exempt by design
explain: W^X says a page is never writable and executable at the same moment. An always-RWX page gives any write bug a place to put code that will run. The recommended pattern is to write, then switch the page to read and execute only.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Control-flow integrity: checking where indirect calls land
question: Why do most Clang CFI schemes require link-time optimization (-flto)?
options: Because LTO makes the binary smaller
Because the set of valid targets for each indirect call depends on every function in the program, which is only visible when the whole program is linked
Because CFI checks run in the linker at run time
Because LTO disables ASLR
explain: Each call site's allowed set includes all address-taken functions of the right type across all object files. Only at link time, with the whole program visible, can the compiler build those sets and emit tight checks.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
question: Android enabled UBSan integer-overflow checks across the media stack. What happens at run time when a crafted file makes `size + chunk_size` overflow?
options: The sum silently wraps and the copy overflows, as before
The check detects the overflow and the process aborts, turning a heap overflow into a crash
The compiler rejects the file
The value is clamped to SIZE_MAX and parsing continues
explain: The sanitizer inserts a check after the addition; on overflow it aborts. Abort is a denial of service at worst, while the unchecked version led to heap corruption and possible code execution.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
question: Core 0 holds line L in Exclusive state and writes to it. What must happen first?
options: Nothing: Exclusive means no other copy exists, so the line silently becomes Modified
An RFO is broadcast to invalidate other copies
The line is written back to main memory
Core 0 must first move the line to Shared
explain: That is the whole point of the Exclusive state: Drepper notes a local write in E does not have to be announced, and that E to M is much faster than S to M. Trouble starts only once another core also wants the line.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
question: In cross-device federated learning, which expectation is realistic for a single round?
options: Every device in the population contributes once per round
The same few hundred devices are reused every round so they can carry state
A few hundred devices are chosen from the much larger set currently available, and some of them will not report back
Devices are addressed by identifier so the server can retry a specific one
explain: Availability is the constraint. Tens of thousands of devices may be checking in, the server picks a few hundred, clients are not individually addressable and are treated as stateless, and 5 percent or more of a round's participants are expected to drop out. Carrying per-client state across rounds is a cross-silo luxury.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
question: Under secure aggregation with 500 clients in a round, what does an honest-but-curious server learn?
options: Each client's update, but only in encrypted form it cannot use
The sum of the 500 masked updates, from which it can subtract any client it chooses
Nothing at all, including the sum, until a trusted third party decrypts it
The sum of the 500 updates and nothing about any individual update
explain: The functionality is exactly summation: the server learns the sum and no individual contribution. It cannot subtract one client out, because each client's value is covered by masks that only cancel in the full sum, and the per-user mask b_u blocks the attack of falsely declaring a live client dropped.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
question: In the codetrace, why is J returned even though J is not in H's stored list?
options: J is H's entry point on the level
J was recovered from H's compressed M_beta entries
Truncation to M adds the next closest node
The lookup reads failing neighbor G's list and J passes the predicate
explain: ACORN-1 expands every neighbor u of H, including ones that fail, into u's own list, then filters. G fails but links to J, so J appears. There is no M_beta compression in ACORN-1 (it is fixed at M_beta = M).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
question: DeepSeek-V3 relies on the bias method yet still keeps a sequence-wise balance loss with alpha = 0.0001. What is the best justification?
options: The bias method does not work without an auxiliary loss
The bias balances load across whole batches; the tiny loss only guards against extreme imbalance within a single sequence, while staying too weak to cause meaningful interference gradients
The loss replaces the bias during the final 500B tokens
It is needed to train the router weights at all
explain: The report calls it complementary: the main balancing is aux-loss-free, and the sequence-wise term exists just to avoid extreme per-sequence imbalance. Its alpha is ten times smaller than the 0.001 baseline used in the loss-free paper. Router weights are trained by the language-modeling loss through the gate values.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately
question: Your FA3-style kernel spills registers after you enlarge the key block size $B_c$ from 128 to 176. Which part of the 2-stage pipeline is most directly to blame?
options: The extra $S_{next}$ buffer of $B_r \times B_c$ FP32 values kept in registers
The TMA descriptors, which grow with $B_c$
The circular SMEM buffer, which lives in registers
The log-sum-exp vector, which grows with $B_c$
explain: The paper calls out exactly this tradeoff: the 2-stage pipeline holds an extra $S_{next}$ of size $B_r \times B_c \times$ sizeof(float) per thread block, which competes with larger block sizes. SMEM buffers are not in registers, and the log-sum-exp has one value per query row ($B_r$), not per key.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
question: Why can FlashInfer's FA3 (Hopper) kernel use TMA for contiguous KV but not for a page table with small pages?
options: TMA does not support FP16
TMA cannot write to shared memory
Paged KV is stored on the CPU
TMA only performs fixed-stride copies, while page gathers follow arbitrary indices
explain: The paper notes Hopper's TMA supports only affine, fixed-stride access patterns. A page table sends consecutive pages to arbitrary addresses, so the kernel computes each address from kv_indices and issues Ampere-style async copies, which costs registers and forces a smaller KV tile.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise
question: Why was maximum-likelihood training of continuous normalizing flows expensive compared with flow matching?
options: The loss required simulating the ODE (and backpropagating through it) on every training step
The network had to output a full probability density instead of a velocity
Maximum likelihood cannot be used with Gaussian noise
It needed a discriminator network as in a GAN
explain: Likelihood training of a CNF integrates the ODE inside the training loop. Flow matching regresses the network onto a closed-form target velocity at a sampled point, so no simulation happens during training.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Which statement best describes the relation between diffusion models and flow matching?
options: They are unrelated; diffusion requires an SDE and cannot be sampled with an ODE
Diffusion paths are Gaussian conditional paths within the flow matching framework, and diffusion models can be sampled with the probability flow ODE
Flow matching is a special case of DDPM with a different noise schedule
Flow matching can only learn straight paths, diffusion can learn curved ones
explain: Lipman et al. recover VE and VP diffusion paths as Gaussian conditional paths, and Song et al.'s probability flow ODE gives diffusion models a deterministic sampler. The marginal flow of any of these, including OT paths, can be curved.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
question: In the TLAPS proof, which assumption lets the same proof cover 3, 5 or 1,001 acceptors?
options: AllowRestart = FALSE
Any two quorums intersect
Values has exactly two elements
TypeOK
explain: Step <1>3 needs one acceptor in both quorums, and QuorumsMeet supplies it for any size. NoRestart is needed too, but it is about the environment, not the size. The proof never mentions how many acceptors or values exist.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
question: A Verus project verifies cleanly, yet in production the service corrupts data. Which explanation is NOT possible if Verus and Z3 are sound?
options: The top-level ensures clause did not state the property that matters
The verified exec function returned a value violating its ensures clause on some input
A trusted spec of an external crate was wrong
The code contains assume(...) that is false
explain: If the tools are sound and nothing false is assumed, every verified function satisfies its ensures on every input. Failures come from what was assumed or trusted, or from specs that say the wrong thing.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
question: An FP8 GEMM with K = 8192 shows growing error versus a BF16 reference, even though inputs are well scaled. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The scales are stale; switch to delayed scaling
Too few mantissa bits in the inputs; switch all inputs to E5M2
Limited-precision accumulation inside the tensor cores; promote partial sums to FP32 every N_C elements
The output is BF16; write it in FP8 instead
explain: The DeepSeek report traces large-K error to about 14-bit accumulation in Hopper FP8 tensor cores and fixes it by moving partial sums to FP32 on CUDA cores every 128 elements. E5M2 inputs would make precision worse, not better.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
question: A tensor has amax 10. One block's amax is 0.05. What is that block's ideal scale before E4M3 rounding, in the stored (multiplied) form?
options: 448, like every block
explain: First s_enc = 6 x 448 / 10 = 268.8. The block's decode scale is 0.05 / 6 = 0.00833, and the stored value is 0.00833 x 268.8 = 2.24, comfortably inside E4M3's range. Without the tensor scale, 0.0083 would sit in E4M3's subnormal region.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
question: During redo, a record for page P has LSN 500. The page as read from disk has page LSN 730. What does recovery do?
options: Apply the record, since redo replays every record after the checkpoint
Stop recovery: the page is newer than the log, so it is corrupt
Skip the record: the page already contains this change and later ones
Roll the page back to LSN 500
explain: The page was written after records up to 730 were applied, so the change at 500 is already in it. Applying only when the record LSN exceeds the page LSN is what makes redo safe to repeat.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Fuzzing from a stormy night in 1988: random, mutation, generation
question: A format starts with a 4-byte magic number and a CRC (checksum) over the whole file. Which fuzzer family is most likely to get past both checks with no extra help?
options: Pure random bytes
Generation from a model that computes the CRC for every input
Mutation of valid seeds, with no knowledge of the CRC
All three are equally likely
explain: Mutation keeps the magic but almost every mutation breaks the CRC, so the parser rejects it early. A generator that knows the format recomputes the checksum, so its inputs reach the code behind it. (libFuzzer's docs suggest a third route: a fuzzing build that skips checksum verification.)

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Sanitizers as oracles: which bug each one catches
question: A fuzzing campaign on a multithreaded image decoder has run under ASan for a week with no reports. Which bug class is it most likely still missing entirely?
options: Heap buffer overflows
Data races and reads of uninitialised memory
Use-after-free
Stack buffer overflows
explain: ASan covers out-of-bounds and use-after-free. Races need a TSan build and uninitialised reads need an MSan build (on Linux), and neither can be combined with ASan.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
question: Why does ClusterFuzz bisect each crash to a commit range?
options: To decide the CVE number
To tell maintainers which change introduced the bug, which speeds up the fix and shows which releases are affected
To make the fuzzer run faster
Bisection removes duplicate crashes
explain: Knowing the introducing commit narrows the search for the root cause and answers the first question users ask: which versions are vulnerable?

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Variant analysis and patch diffing: one bug, many siblings
question: You fixed a missing length check in one message handler. What is the variant-analysis step?
options: Wait for a fuzzer to find other bugs
Describe the pattern (input length used without a destination bound) and search every handler for it, then triage the hits
Add a CVE number
Rewrite the fixed handler in another language
explain: Variant analysis uses the understood bug as a seed. The search can be a CodeQL query, a grep or a focused review; the point is to look for the same mistake everywhere.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
question: A teammate initializes the first row as `prev = [0] * (len(b) + 1)` instead of `list(range(len(b) + 1))`. What does the function now compute?
options: The same Levenshtein distance, because row 0 is overwritten anyway
The cost of matching `a` against the best substring of `b` that ends at its last character, because skipping a prefix of `b` becomes free
Always 0
The longest common subsequence length
explain: Row 0 says how much it costs to consume a prefix of `b` before `a` starts. Setting it to 0 makes that free, so a match may start anywhere in `b`. Sellers used exactly this change in 1980 to turn the distance algorithm into approximate substring search. It is a useful algorithm, but not Levenshtein distance.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: A Levenshtein automaton for query `fuzzy` with k = 1 reaches a state where every entry of the DP row is 2 after reading `ja`. Why can it reject every term starting with `ja` without reading further?
options: Because terms starting with ja are rare
Because the row minimum never decreases as more characters are read, so the final distance will be at least 2
Because the automaton only accepts terms of exactly 5 characters
Because Lucene sets prefix_length to 2
explain: Each new cell is at least the minimum of the previous row (diagonal moves add 0 or 1, the others add 1), so a row whose minimum is 2 can only lead to distances of 2 or more. That dead state lets the engine skip the entire ja block of the sorted term dictionary.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Searching code space: kd-trees, tolerance and why quads beat triangles
question: You double the code-match tolerance to cope with a noisy camera. In the uniform toy model, by what factor do chance matches per query grow for quads?
options: 2x
4x
8x
explain: The query region is a 4D ball whose volume grows as t to the 4th power, so doubling t multiplies chance matches by 16. For 2D triangle codes it would be 4x. This is why quads tolerate a larger index before verification costs explode.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
question: A ship-tracking query in Fiji uses the filter lon ≥ 179.5 AND lon ≤ -179.5 to find ships within about 50 km of the antimeridian. It returns zero rows even though ships are there. What is the fix?
options: Swap the bounds to lon ≥ -179.5 AND lon ≤ 179.5
Convert longitudes to radians before comparing
Split the box into two: lon ≥ 179.5 OR lon ≤ -179.5
Use a larger box so the bounds no longer cross 180
explain: The interval wraps around 180, so no single number is both at least 179.5 and at most -179.5. The correct region is the union of two ranges. Swapping the bounds selects almost the whole planet instead, and a larger box still wraps.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Tree indexes: R-trees, PostGIS GiST and Lucene BKD
question: A PostGIS query uses `geom && query_box` to count census blocks in a neighborhood and gets a much larger number than expected. Why?
options: The GiST index is stale and needs VACUUM ANALYZE
&& compares bounding boxes only, so blocks whose boxes touch the neighborhood's box are counted even if the shapes do not intersect
&& uses meters while the data is in degrees
&& rounds coordinates to 4-byte integers
explain: && is the index-only bounding box test. It is the fast first pass; an exact predicate like ST_Intersects must refine the result. Statistics affect the plan's speed, not which rows match.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Color conversion: a 3x3 matrix per pixel, with the right coefficients
question: A grayscale conversion of HD footage uses the 0.299, 0.587, 0.114 row. What is the effect?
options: Any non-neutral pixel's luma is biased, by 13 levels for a mid green-ish pixel and up to about 32 levels for saturated green
No effect, since luma rows differ only by a scale factor
Only saturated reds change, because red's coefficient differs the most
The image becomes brighter overall by a constant offset that can be subtracted out
explain: The rows are not proportional: green goes from 0.587 to 0.7152 and blue from 0.114 to 0.0722. The error depends on the pixel's hue, so it is neither a constant offset nor confined to one channel. For our four sample pixels the gap ranges from 1 to 32 levels, with green worst because its weight moved most.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
question: In the final state, memory_allocated() reports 27 MiB but tensors requested only 25 MiB. Where did the 2 extra MiB go?
options: Two unsplit leftovers of 1 MiB each, attached to D and F
Event bookkeeping for streams
The rounding of 7 MiB up to 8 MiB
Metadata headers stored in device memory
explain: D asked for 4 MiB and got a 5 MiB block; F asked for 14 MiB and got 15 MiB. In both cases the remainder (1 MiB) was not more than 1 MiB, so the large pool refused to split. allocated_bytes counts whole blocks; requested_bytes counts what tensors asked for.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
question: Which level of the hierarchy is shared by every SM on the GPU?
options: Shared memory
The L2 cache
The register file
The L1 cache
explain: Shared memory, L1 and registers are per SM. The Programming Guide describes L2 as located on the device and shared among all the SMs, which is why one kernel's wasteful traffic can slow every other SM.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
question: A teammate drops `__syncthreads()` from the tiled transpose because "each thread only touches its own data." What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the barrier only affects performance
Threads read tile elements written by other warps, so they may read before those writes happen
Without the barrier the global writes become uncoalesced
The barrier is needed only when the tile is padded
explain: Thread (x, y) stores tile[y+j][x] but later reads tile[x][y+j], an element another thread, often in another warp, stored. The NVIDIA transpose post requires `__syncthreads()` because threads write different data to odata than they read from idata, and the CUDA guide says synchronization is necessary when threads of a block share shared memory addresses.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
question: You profile with `--set full` and the application takes 30 times longer, but the reported kernel durations are unchanged. What is the right reading?
options: The durations are stale and should be taken from Nsight Systems instead
The kernels have become slower and the tool is hiding it
Expected: a full metric set needs many replay passes plus save, restore and flush around each, none of which is included in the reported duration
Software-patched metrics have inflated the reported duration
explain: More metrics means more passes, and the per-pass preparation and post-processing is explicitly not included in the reported duration. The documentation notes the same thing in reverse: because of that overhead you cannot derive a kernel's duration from host timers or CUDA events while profiling with Nsight Compute. Duration is also never collected in a software-patching pass, so those metrics do not distort it.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
question: A kernel uses a 48 KB shared-memory tile and `__syncthreads()`. A teammate proposes having block 7 read the tile that block 3 just loaded, to save a global memory read. When is that allowed?
options: Always: shared memory is shared by the whole grid
Never, under any launch configuration
Only if blocks 3 and 7 are in the same thread block cluster, using distributed shared memory and cluster.sync() on compute capability 9.0 or later
Only if both blocks call __syncthreads() first
explain: Ordinary shared memory is private to one block. Clusters (compute capability 9.0 and later) let blocks in the same cluster map each other's shared memory, because the cluster's blocks are co-scheduled. With a portable cluster size of at most 8, blocks 3 and 7 would need a cluster shape that contains both, which a 1D cluster of 8 starting at block 0 does. __syncthreads() never reaches across blocks.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
question: After merging, the node QUILLFERN LABS has descriptions from 3 chunks and BEN ORTIZ has one. How many description-summarization LLM calls do these two nodes need?
explain: Only lists with more than one description are sent to the LLM. QUILLFERN LABS needs 1 call; BEN ORTIZ keeps its single description as is.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
question: In HippoRAG's PPR step, why does Quillfern Labs score high for the question about Ben Ortiz and Rover X2, even though the question never mentions it?
options: Because random walks restarting at both seeds pass through it, so it collects probability from both sides
Because it has the longest description
Because the LLM ranked it first
Because it is in the largest community
explain: PPR mass flows outward from the seed nodes. A node adjacent to both seeds receives probability from each, which is how the bridge in a multi-hop chain surfaces without an extra retrieval round.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: The GRPO objective token by token: clipping, averaging and KL
question: In DeepSeekMath's setup the policy takes exactly one gradient step per batch of sampled outputs. What does the clip term do in that step?
options: It clips every token whose advantage is negative
It halves the learning rate for long outputs
It replaces the KL penalty
Nothing: the ratio is exactly 1, so the clipped and unclipped terms are equal
explain: With one update per batch, pi_theta equals pi_old when the loss is evaluated, so every ratio is 1, well inside [1 - eps, 1 + eps]. The objective reduces to a policy gradient weighted by the group advantages, plus the KL term.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Service days, calendar exceptions and times past 24:00
question: A feed has WKDY in calendar.txt (Mon to Fri) and a row WKDY, 20260704, exception_type 1 for Saturday July 4. What happens on July 4?
options: Nothing, Saturdays are 0 in calendar.txt so the exception is ignored
The feed is invalid because the date is outside the weekly pattern
Only trips with times past 24:00:00 run
All WKDY trips run on July 4 as an added service day
explain: exception_type 1 adds service on that date even though the weekly pattern says no. calendar_dates.txt modifies calendar.txt; that is exactly how special event or holiday services are added.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
question: A hot function has IPC 0.25 and 20 last-level cache misses per 1000 instructions. Which change is most likely to make it faster?
options: Rewrite it to execute 10% fewer instructions with the same memory access pattern
Change the data layout so consecutive iterations touch the same cache lines
Compile with a higher optimization level to shorten the instruction sequence
Run it on a core with a wider decoder
explain: Low IPC with many cache misses means the core is mostly waiting on memory. Removing instructions or widening the front end does little while every miss still stalls. Better locality cuts the misses that the cycles are actually spent on.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
question: TopdownL1 shows 60% backend bound, and drilling down shows most of it is memory bound. IPC is 0.4. Which next step fits best?
options: Reduce branch mispredictions with likely/unlikely hints
Shrink the binary so it fits in the instruction cache
Sample a cache-miss event with :pp to find the loads responsible, then improve their locality
Ignore it: backend bound means the CPU is doing useful work
explain: Memory bound means slots are lost waiting on data. Bad speculation and frontend fixes target other buckets. Precise sampling on a miss event points at the exact loads to restructure.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Branchless selection and secret-independent memory access
question: Which line breaks rule 2 (no secret-dependent memory addresses)?
options: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += table[i];
mask = 0u - secret_bit;
out = sbox[key_byte ^ plaintext_byte];
if (len != 32) return -1;  /* len is public */
explain: The sbox index depends on the key, so the cache line touched depends on the key. The loop over all entries uses public indices, the mask is pure arithmetic, and the length check branches on a public value.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Meltdown: reading kernel memory, and why KPTI fixes it
question: Why does KPTI stop Meltdown but not Spectre variant 1?
options: KPTI disables speculation in user mode
KPTI flushes the cache on every system call
Meltdown reads kernel memory that is mapped but forbidden; KPTI unmaps it, while Spectre makes the victim read its own mapped memory
Spectre does not use the cache
explain: With the kernel unmapped there is no translation for a transient load to use. Spectre variant 1 abuses the victim's own legitimate mappings, so removing other mappings changes nothing.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels
question: Why did Hertzbleed affect code that was written to be constant-time?
options: CPU frequency scaling depends on power draw, which depends on data, so the same instructions run at different speeds for different data
The code had a secret-dependent branch
SIKE used lookup tables
The attack needed physical access to measure power
explain: Constant-time rules control which instructions and addresses run. Hertzbleed changes how fast the same instructions run, through data-dependent power and frequency, and needs no power probe.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a 2 MiB mapping: offset bits, alignment, contiguity
question: A server with 40 GiB of free memory runs `echo 10000 > /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages` (2 MiB pages, 19.5 GiB) and the pool only reaches 3,100 pages. What is the most likely cause?
options: nr_hugepages is capped at 3,100 by default
Huge pages count against swap, which is full
Free memory is fragmented, so few aligned 2 MiB runs of free frames exist
The kernel only allows huge pages up to 10% of RAM
explain: Allocation success depends on physically contiguous memory at the time of the request, as the hugetlb docs state. Retrying after compaction or allocating at boot (hugepages=N) works better. There is no default cap of that kind, and hugetlb pages are not swappable at all.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
question: A pure SSM answers a phone-book query with 555-284-7710 when the true number is 555-284-7719. What does this suggest?
options: The entry was compressed into the fixed state but cannot be read back exactly
The model never saw the entry, so it guessed a random number
The tokenizer split the digits incorrectly
The model needs positional embeddings to count digits
explain: Waleffe et al. found SSM answers share many digits with the correct number: information about each entry is in the state, but crosstalk from everything else blurs it. That is the capacity limit of a fixed-size memory, not missing information.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
question: Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B has 12 full attention layers, each with 2 KV heads of dimension 256. How much KV cache does one token need in 16-bit?
options: 6 KiB
12 KiB
192 KiB
24 KiB
explain: 2 (K and V) x 12 layers x 2 heads x 256 x 2 bytes = 24,576 bytes = 24 KiB. At 262,144 tokens that is 6 GiB, plus the fixed Gated DeltaNet state of the other 36 layers.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
question: Zamba-7B applies one shared attention block at 13 depths. Compared with 13 separate attention layers of the same shape, its KV cache is:
options: 13x smaller, since the weights are shared
Zero, since shared layers need no cache
Half as large
The same size, since each call sees different activations
explain: Weights are shared, activations are not: each call computes its own keys and values from a different residual stream, so each needs its own cache. The Zamba paper states this directly (independent KV-cache entries at each invocation), and so does Zamba2's report; the saving is in parameters.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Choosing a fusion method and running it at scale
question: You have 300 labeled queries from your domain and two retrievers. Based on Bruch et al., which fusion is the better starting point?
options: A convex combination with alpha tuned on the labeled queries
RRF with k = 60, because it never needs tuning
Raw score sum, since labels make normalization unnecessary
Whichever retriever is better alone, without fusion
explain: Their study found a tuned convex combination outperformed RRF in and out of domain, and that a small labeled set suffices to tune alpha. RRF remains a good zero-shot default when you have no labels.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
question: Users of an internal tool type short product code names that the LLM has never seen. HyDE with N=8 is underperforming plain dense retrieval. What is the best first change?
options: Give the raw query far more weight, or skip HyDE for these queries: every sample shares the same misreading, so averaging cannot fix it
Raise N to 32 so the noise averages out
Raise the temperature for more diverse passages
Switch the encoder for the hypothetical passages only
explain: Unfamiliar names produce a shared bias, which more samples cannot remove (lesson 3), and N=8 even shrinks the query's weight to 1/9. Routing these queries to plain or lexical retrieval, or weighting the query up, addresses the cause. Switching encoders breaks the shared embedding space.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: The Purdue model: levels from field devices to the enterprise
question: Under NIST's Purdue guidance, how should business users get production numbers from the plant historian?
options: Connect directly to the Level 3 historian from Level 4
Email the operators
Query the PLCs directly so the data is fresher
Read a replica of the historian in the DMZ, which the plant pushes data to
explain: Data is handed over in the DMZ so no business system connects into the control network. A replica historian (pushed from inside, ideally one way) is the classic pattern; lesson 13 adds unidirectional gateways.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
question: Which single check would have caught the attack earliest in the scenario?
options: Waiting for the HMI high-level alarm
A monthly review of historian trends
A monitoring rule on Modbus writes from hosts other than the HMI
Rebooting the HMI
explain: The write happened at minute 10 and produced a network event at once. The HMI alarm would never fire because the HMI showed replayed data, and monthly reviews are far too slow.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
question: What made the Unitronics compromises possible, according to CISA?
options: A zero-day in Modbus
Stolen certificates
Internet-facing PLCs with default or no passwords on default ports
Insider sabotage
explain: No advanced exploit was needed. Removing the devices from the internet and changing default passwords would have stopped this campaign; CISA's primary mitigations list exactly these.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
question: A company moves 30 apps behind one IdP. Which statement is true?
options: MFA and offboarding now happen in one place, and that place becomes the most valuable account system to attack
The apps can now verify Ana's MFA themselves
Each app no longer needs a session of its own
Password phishing becomes impossible
explain: Centralising login concentrates both benefit and risk: one place to enforce MFA and remove access, and one key that every app trusts. Apps still keep their own sessions, and the IdP's own login page can still be phished unless MFA is phishing-resistant.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Validating a SAML response: every check, and the replay cache
question: An SP checks the signature, Issuer and time window, but not the Audience. Which attack does that allow?
options: A malicious or compromised SP that receives the user's assertions can replay them to this SP and log in as those users
None, the signature is enough
XML signature wrapping
Login CSRF only
explain: Every SP that federates with the same IdP receives genuine, signed assertions about its users. Without the Audience check, any of them (or anyone who breaches one) can present those assertions here. It is the SAML twin of accepting a JWT with someone else's aud.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
question: An SP's library verifies a SAML signature using the certificate in the response's own KeyInfo element. What can an attacker do?
options: Sign an assertion with any key of their own and include its certificate, so verification succeeds
Nothing, the certificate proves who signed
Only replay old assertions
